name: Gaigel
description: Gaigel is a traditional trick-taking game hailing from Swabia in Southwest Germany. Closely related to the game 'Sixty-Six' (Sechsundsechzig), Gaigel is played with a double-deck of 48 cards, typically featuring the distinct German-suited WÃ¼rttemberg pattern. It is primarily a partnership game where the goal is to reach 101 card points through captured tricks and 'marriages' (King and Ober pairs). The game is famous for its midndgame shift, where strict following-suit rules only apply once the draw pile (Talon) is exhausted.

history.origins: Gaigel originated in the 19th century in the Swabian region of Germany. It is named after its highest rank (the 'Gaigel' or Ace in some dialects). It co-evolved with Binokel and represents a rich tradition of Southwestern German pub games.
timeline: 1800s: Traditional Swabian rules formalize into the modern version.
1900s: Becomes the 'national' card game of the Swabian population, alongside Schafkopf.
2018: Featured at the International PlayingndCard Society convention in Leinfelden, solidifying its status as an established classic.
Present: Extensively played in Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg and by German communities abroad.
history.cultural: In Swabian pubs, Gaigel is often played for 'Striche' (marks) on a chalkboard, representing rounds won.
history.evolution: The game uses two identical copies of every card, making it a precursor to games like Pinochle and Doppelkopf.

setup.players: 4 players in two partnerships (North/South vs East/West).
setup.deck: 48 cards (WÃ¼rttemberg pattern). Two copies of Ace, 10, King, Ober, Unter, and 7 per suit.
setup.dealing: Done counter-clockwise in batches of 3 then 2. The 21st card is turned face-up as the trump suit indicator.

rules.objective: The aim of the play is to take tricks containing valuable cards and to declare King-Ober marriages; the first team that reaches 101 or more points wins the round and must stop the play by calling Aus to claim the win.
rules.gameplay: Gaigel proceeds through deal, legal play actions, and end-of-round resolution. Play proceeds through legal actions until round resolution.
keyRules: Out! (Schluss!): A player can stop the game midndhand if they believe their team has reached 101 points. If they are correct, they win. If they are wrong, the opponents win regardless of the final score.
Round outcome is resolved by the scoring method: Scoring summary: Points scored through tricks and marriage declarations.
Winning condition: First team to reach 101 points wins the round.

strategy.basic: In Phase 1, use your 7s to throw away junk cards and win tricks with your Aces to draw fresh cards from the Talon. Don't waste high cards until the Talon is nearly empty.
strategy.intermediate: Count the 10s. Since 10s are worth 10 points but rank below Aces, they are easy to lose if you lead them too early. Try to 'duck' tricks that contain 10s unless you are sure you can win.
strategy.advanced: Phase 2 Preparation: Watch which cards your partner is 'throwing' during Phase 1. If they throw a 7 of Hearts, it's a signal to play Hearts in Phase 2 because they are likely void or holding trumps to protect that suit.
tips: If you have a Trump Marriage (K+O), declare it immediately on your lead. 40 points is nearly 40% of the way to victory.
Know when to stop the game. If you've been tracking tricks and know you are at 101, call 'Out!' before your opponent can catch up.

scoring.description: Points scored through tricks and marriage declarations. First team to 101 points wins the round.
scoring.winCondition: A side wins by correctly declaring Aus at 101 or more points; incorrect Aus loses double and overgaigeln can also cause a double loss.

synthesis.shortDescription: A partnership trick-taking game from Southwest Germany combining strategic play in two distinct phases: free play while cards remain in the Talon, then strict suit-following once the Talon is exhausted.
